reviews.scope: corresponding length and surface-area ratio comparisons
reviews.reason: Relating linear scale factors to squared surface-area multipliers requires understanding a ratio as the multiplicative quotient comparing corresponding measurements of two similar solids.

reviews.scope: quadratic scaling analogy between planar regions and solid surfaces
reviews.reason: Planar area scaling establishes why two-dimensional measures grow with the square of linear dimensions, motivating why solid surface area follows a quadratic rather than cubic law.
reviews.counterexample: One can apply the three-dimensional surface-area scaling law directly to curved or polyhedral solids without first solving planar similarity tasks.

reviews.scope: sphere surface-area and volume scaling as a concrete prototype
reviews.reason: Comparing sphere surface areas and volumes across radii provides a concrete example contrasting quadratic surface scaling with cubic volume scaling before generalizing to arbitrary similar solids.
reviews.counterexample: General surface-area scaling for similar solids or statues can be applied directly from linear scale factors without using sphere formulas.

reviews.scope: convert scaled surface area into constant-rate coating quantity
reviews.reason: When surface-area scaling is extended to paint or coating consumption at a fixed coverage rate, direct proportion links total surface area to required material quantity.
reviews.counterexample: Pure surface-area ratio problems compare geometric areas directly without introducing a constant-rate material coating model.

reviews.scope: identifying a sphere and its radius parameter
reviews.reason: Applying the sphere volume formula or recovering a radius from given volume data requires knowing the geometric meaning of a sphere and its radius.

reviews.scope: expressing sphere volume in consistent cubic units
reviews.reason: Computing and comparing three-dimensional sphere volumes from linear radius measurements requires understanding cubic volume units and maintaining unit consistency across calculations.

reviews.scope: volume comparisons between a sphere and a cone
reviews.reason: Comparing the volume of a sphere with that of a cone or relating their dimensions requires the cone volume formula of one-third base area times height.
reviews.counterexample: Computing standalone sphere volume or comparing a sphere with a cylinder or cube does not involve cone volume.

reviews.scope: normal-curve symmetry and parameter roles before standardizing to N(0,1)
reviews.reason: Understanding how the mean sets the symmetry axis and the variance governs spread for general normal curves prepares students to interpret the standard parameter choice N(0,1).
reviews.counterexample: One can identify the mean 0, variance 1, and symmetric interval endpoints [-k, k] directly from the definition of N(0,1) without qualitative variance comparisons.

reviews.scope: symmetric standard-deviation intervals contrasted with empirical coverage percentages
reviews.reason: Working with one- and two-sigma intervals in the empirical rule familiarizes students with standard-deviation interval notation while helping distinguish interval endpoints from approximate coverage probabilities.
reviews.counterexample: Finding the endpoints -k and k for k standard deviations around mean 0 in N(0,1) does not require approximate 68% or 95% coverage rules.

reviews.scope: vector concept, magnitude meaning, and contrast with zero vector
reviews.reason: Defining a unit vector by having magnitude equal to one and distinguishing it from the zero vector requires knowing what a vector and its magnitude are.

reviews.scope: verifying unit length from planar vector coordinates
reviews.reason: Testing whether a vector given in component form has magnitude one uses the Pythagorean coordinate norm formula from vector magnitude calculations.
reviews.counterexample: A vector whose length is stated directly or given geometrically on a unit circle can be identified as a unit vector without coordinate norm computation.
